newsitem.title: USA: Aetna reports drop in profits, stock tumbles.
newsitem.headline: Aetna reports drop in profits, stock tumbles.

text.p: Aetna Inc., one of the nation's biggest health insurance companies, posted disappointing second quarter results Tuesday, sending the company's stock price down sharply.

Aetna said its net income fell 20 percent in the second quarter to $230.1 million, down from $288 million in the same year-ago period. Excluding charges mainly tied to the write-off of intangible assets, the company reported earnings per share of $1.27, down from $1.43 per share a year ago.

Although the per share figures were in line with Wall Street estimates, the results were overshadowed by a downturn in operating earnings within Aetna's health risk business compared with this year's first quarter, analysts said.

In addition, the company's decision to post $31 million from its reserve fund toward the current quarter's profits inflated earnings by about 12 cents a share, said Smith Barney analyst Geoffrey Harris.
Citing a disappointing performance by the company's managed-care business, Harris lowered his rating on Aetna's stock to "outperform" from "buy."
Aetna's stock slid $12.75, or 10 percent, to $104.25 in early afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was one of the most actively traded issues.

Operating profits within Aetna's health risk segment, which includes products in which the company assumes all or a majority of health care costs and utilization risk, totalled $172 million in the second quarter, down from $198 million in the first quarter of 1997.
The company said higher commercial and Medicare costs more than offset higher premium rates.
Aetna merged with managed care company U.S. Healthcare in July of last year.
Fuelled by the merger, revenues climbed to $4.63 billion in the period, compared with $3.17 billion in last year's second quarter, the company said.
Separately, Oxford Health Plans Inc. said Tuesday its net income surged 66 percent in the second quarter, driven by increased enrollment in its fully insured programmes and stable medical costs.
The Norwalk, Conn.-based health insurer said its profits climbed to $37.2 million in the second quarter, up from $22.5 million posted a year ago.
Earnings per share jumped to 45 cents in the second quarter, up from 28 cents a share a year ago and beating analysts' average estimate by one cent.

But the strong results were not enough to insulate the company's stock from an industry-wide sell off Tuesday. Oxford fell $4.125 to $81.69 in early afternoon trading on Nasdaq, as jitters tied to Aetna's second quarter results spread to other managed care stocks.
"Apparently, the Aetna downgrade (by Smith Barney) was disappointing to investors and Oxford fell off in sympathy," said PaineWebber health care analyst David Lothson.
Oxford said its total revenues reached $1.06 billion for the quarter ended June 30, a 46 percent increase from $725.3 million a year ago.
Oxford also announced that its founder, Stephen Wiggins, had resigned as chief executive but will remain the company's chairman. Acting chief executive William Sullivan was elevated to the CEO spot.
Oxford markets health insurance plans to employers in New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Connecticut and New Hampshire.
